name: Carlos Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm not really a computer person, so I hope that's not a problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Frank Doyle, who's a one-man electrician in a small seaside town, and I'm his only lad. We do callouts mostly: tripping fuses, dead sockets, a light that buzzes, the odd kitchen rewire for the holiday lets. Frank does the thinking and I do the crawling under floors and the carrying. I like a fault that's been driving someone mad for weeks and we find it in ten minutes. What wears me out is the low pay and waiting by the van while Frank chats to the customer for half an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Okay. That's what I'd guessed anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it was just another gadget. I don't post online, but at the pub I'd say the same as most people. I wouldn't make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry. My boss is 61 and talks about retiring every time his knees ache. When my boss stops, my job stops, robots or no robots. There's maybe two other firms in town, and neither has room for someone without a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Frank and try to get him to put me on more of the fault-finding so I learn it. I'd try to put 20 a week away, which I've said before and never managed. That's about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a quiet way. It's always there in the back of my head when I'm in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Frank say about retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank says two years, then three, then two again. His wife wants to move nearer their daughter. He's never once said what happens to me, and I've never asked, because I don't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you managed to save the 20 before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's 650, the van insurance comes out of my wage because I drive to Frank's, and Lucy, my partner, is on part-time hours at the supermarket. By the end of the month it's gone. I'm not careless, there's just nothing left.

say: I'd say AI was just **another gadget** that got talked up too much.
I'd keep it to **the pub** with my mates, not online.
think: My boss Frank is **61** and may retire, which would end my job.
Only **two other firms** in town, and neither hires unlicensed electricians.
do: Keep working for Frank and ask to do more of the **fault-finding** myself.
Try again to save **20 a week**, which I've never managed before.
feel: Anxious in a **quiet** way that never really goes away.
S0.quote: My boss is 61 and talks about retiring every time his knees ache. When my boss stops, my job stops, robots or no robots.
fieldNote: His job hangs on **one ageing boss**, not on technology.
He **avoids asking** about Frank's plans because he fears the answer.
Savings fail from **tight bills**, not carelessness.

steps.text: Ask Frank to let him lead the fault-finding on callouts
Set up a 20-a-week standing order to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. Frank doesn't do much on a computer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably good for some people and bad for others, and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions. At the pub I'd say the office lot should be worried, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think it touches my bit of the job much. Computers can do the quotes if they want. A computer can't find the dodgy junction box behind a bathroom tile in a house built in 1962. What might happen is Frank's nephew gets him on some app and he gets busier, or he decides it's easier to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing different at first. I'd wait and see if it actually changes the callouts. If Frank brought in an app, I'd let him deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about Lucy more than me. The supermarket's already got more self-checkouts than tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Frank deal with the app. What if Frank retired and a new boss needed you to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to, I suppose, but I'd be bad at it. I can barely work my banking app. I'd probably ask Lucy to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Lucy's hours in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy's on 20 hours already and they keep trimming. If AI answers customers and orders stock, there's less for the shop floor staff. If Lucy drops to 12 hours, we're short on rent.

say: I'd say AI is **good for some**, bad for others.
I'd say the **office workers** should worry, not tradespeople.
think: Software won't find a **faulty junction box** behind a bathroom tile.
Lucy's supermarket **hours** are more at risk than my job.
do: **Wait and see** whether the callouts actually change before doing anything.
Leave any new booking or quoting app to **Frank** to deal with.
feel: Worried for **Lucy** more than for myself, with our rent at stake.
S1.quote: Computers can do the quotes if they want. A computer can't find the dodgy junction box behind a bathroom tile in a house built in 1962.
fieldNote: He feels his **hands-on tasks** are safe in this picture.
The household risk is **Lucy's hours** at the supermarket.
He avoids technology and would **lean on his partner** to learn an app.

steps.text: Wait to see if callouts drop before changing anything
Keep doing the crawling and cabling for Frank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's really soon. I'm still learning the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody asked for this and it's being rushed. I'd say both the government and the big firms should slow down. I wouldn't march or anything, though, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done. I don't know anything about AI, and by 2028 it'd be too late to start learning. I'd just be a pair of hands waiting for the robots. Frank would retire the minute the quoting and bookings went to an app, because he likes the chatting part, not the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no van insurance if I can avoid driving, no takeaway, cancel the phone contract. I'd ask my parents if we could move back to their place if it came to it. I'd look at labouring jobs, which pay even less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent 650, Lucy's wage maybe 900 if she keeps her hours, my wage gone. That's not enough for food and bills. So it's my mum's spare room, which Lucy would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's being rushed. Who should slow it down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the government, but also the firms. I'm not one of those people who blames one side. Everyone's in it for themselves.

say: I'd say this is being **rushed** and nobody asked for it.
I'd say both **government and big firms** should slow down.
think: By 2028 it's **too late** for me to learn AI.
Frank would **retire** as soon as quotes and bookings moved to an app.
do: **Cut** the phone contract, takeaways and van insurance.
Ask my parents about **moving back** in.
S2.quote: I don't know anything about AI, and by 2028 it'd be too late to start learning. I'd just be a pair of hands waiting for the robots.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** soon after 2028, when Frank retires.
He has no tech skills and **sees no way in**.
His plan is about **cutting costs** and family help, not retraining.

steps.text: Cancel the phone contract and stop takeaways
Ask Mum and Dad about moving into their spare room
Apply for labouring jobs on local building sites

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. A bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't that long but it's something. I'd say people should get on with training while there's time. I'd probably say it and not do it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still worry about Frank retiring around then anyway. I'm not going to be the bloke with the robot. I'd rather be the bloke the robot company calls when its machine can't get into a loft. Old houses are awkward, every one's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending a bit, start saving properly, and maybe finally ask Frank about the licence. But mostly I'd keep my head down and see what happens to other electricians first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but less so than with two years. There's time, I'm just not sure I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably say it and not do it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I've done with the licence for three years. I'm not lazy, I'm scared of the classroom. And it costs money I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Frank sat me down and said he's retiring in 2029. Then I'd have no choice. Or if someone paid for the course.

say: I'd say five years **isn't long** but it's something.
I'd tell people to get **training** while there's time.
think: Frank will probably **retire around then** anyway, whatever happens with AI.
Robots will struggle with **awkward old houses** for a while, because each is different.
do: **Wait** to see what happens to other electricians.
S3.quote: I'm not going to be the bloke with the robot. I'd rather be the bloke the robot company calls when its machine can't get into a loft.
fieldNote: He admits he'd likely **say and not do**, as with the licence.
He'd only move if **forced** by Frank or helped with costs.
He hopes **old housing** keeps robots out longer.

steps.text: Drop the gym membership and save the difference
Wait and see how other electricians cope before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, that's time to sort yourself out. At the pub I'd say anyone who's caught out by that has only themselves to blame. Then I'd feel a bit guilty saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd push me to do what I should do anyway. Ten years means I can stop putting off the licence. Nobody can say I didn't get a warning. I'd still be scared of the classroom, but less scared than of being 40 with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the licence course in the next year and pay monthly. I'd try to take over some of Frank's customers when he retires, maybe with Lucy doing the bookings. I'd save what I could, even 15 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious that gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for bookings and quotes if you took over Frank's customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not me, but Lucy would. Lucy's quicker on a phone than I am. I'd do the work, she'd do the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty saying people have themselves to blame. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be talking about myself, really. I've had chances and I've let them slide. Ten years would mean I couldn't hide behind not knowing.

say: I'd say ten years is time to **sort yourself out**.
I'd say people caught out have **themselves** to blame, then feel guilty.
think: Ten years pushes me to finally get the **licence**.
Being **40 with nothing** scares me more than the classroom.
do: Sign up for the **licence course** next year, paid monthly.
Try to take over **Frank's customers** with Lucy on bookings.
feel: Anxious, but in a way that **gets me moving**.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can stop putting off the licence. Nobody can say I didn't get a warning.
fieldNote: With a decade, the **licence** finally feels unavoidable.
His harsh public line is really **self-criticism**.
He'd **split the work** with Lucy: his hands, her screen.

steps.text: Enrol in the electrician's licence course and pay monthly
Take over Frank's customers with Lucy handling bookings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and nothing to fall back on. I don't need the future explained to me. I need someone to tell me which course, how much, and who pays my rent while I'm on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old blokes like Frank. Half the electricians round here are near retirement, and the young ones like me only have a job as long as the old ones keep going.

headlineQuote: I don't need the future explained to me. I need someone to tell me which course, how much, and who pays my rent while I'm on it.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old junior**, the only employee of a 61-year-old electrician.
He **never uses AI** and is unsure even on his banking app.
His real worry is his boss **retiring**, and his partner's shrinking supermarket hours.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because he sees no way to catch up in time.
With ten years he'd finally get his **licence** and take on his boss's customers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to change and nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on **which course**, what it costs, and **rent support** while studying.
